cards.definition: a living organism that meets these three criteria: feeds on organic matter; is able to move from one place to another; and is made up of multiple eukaryotic cells and can produce collagen
animals that have a spinal cord, brain, hair, and three middle ear bones and produce milk
Part of the central nervous system, it is the bundle of nerves originating from the brain that allows for quick behavioral responses and reflexive behavior.
describes animals that develop their young internally, giving birth to live young instead of eggs; fertilization occurs only internally
describes animals that lay eggs wherein their young develop further and from which they eventually hatch
describes animals that internally develop their young in eggs before they hatch and give birth to live young

members of the largest phylum in the animal kingdom; includes all insects and arachnids; all arthropods have an open circulatory system, no spinal cord, and an external skeletal system called an exoskeleton.
all the ways in which animals interact with other organisms, internal stimuli, and the physical environment
sensory information that comes from outside of the body
sensory information that comes from inside of the body
all the organisms of the same species in an area
a group of multiple different populations that all exist in an area
a group of multiple communities, including the environment and plants and all interactions between them
a large area encompassing multiple ecosystems that share common environmental conditions
the collection of all environments found on Earth
a species that has a vital role in the ecosystem and is necessary for multiple species to exist
the field of research that seeks to systematically classify organisms with a universally used name and category that gives descriptive information about the organism’s relation to other living things
also known as a taxonomic name; the specific name created in Latin for a species or animal that includes information about its believed relationship with other animals
a visual representation of the evolutionary history of how animals are related to one another
a line on a phylogenetic tree that represents one group of animals or an individual, depending on the type of phylogenetic tree
the point at which two branches meet on a phylogenetic tree, representing the last ancestor shared between the two groups of animals represented by the branches
the point at which two species can no longer breed together due to their genetics becoming too different, and they develop into two separate new species
the total change in a population of organisms over time, including physical and behavioral traits
how successful an individual organism is relative to others at reproducing and passing on its genetic information
a specific, observable characteristic of an organism that can be determined by genes, the environment, or both
the process that drives the evolution of physical or behavioral traits over generations
the factors that affect which traits are inherited in a population; positive selection pressures add new traits to the population, and negative pressures remove traits.
a theory of natural selection that explains why behaviors, like the tendency to help genetically related relatives, persist in some species despite being costly to the individual
the science and study of animal behavior

a type of learning where an animal develops a specific behavioral response to a stimulus necessary for survival at a critical timepoint early in development; if the stimulus is not present during the critical period, the animal will never learn the behavior.
behaviors that animals are born knowing how to do that do not require learning
the human tendency to use human characteristics to explain the behavior or intentions of animals without scientific evidence
a noninvasive way to study the behavior of animals in their natural environment by observing and recording their behavior from a distance

the group of animals in an experiment that does not experience any direct manipulation during a research study; the control group is used to compare what effect the manipulation or treatment has on a behavior.
a description of behaviors observed in an animal; used by researchers to objectively record behaviors
a statistical method of testing how consistent two or more independent observers are in evaluating the same behaviors
the subset of artificial intelligence (AI) focused on algorithms that can “learn” the patterns of training data and, subsequently, make accurate inferences about new data
a type of protein produced by some eukaryotic cells that provides structure to the cells
a type of cell that is surrounded by a membrane and has internal organelles that are also surrounded by a membrane
